I built more 3-statement models by hand at Morgan Stanley than I'd like to admit. Claude in Excel is a game changer .... here's how I build any model in 5 passes:

The process is all about context window management to minimize hardcodes + hallucinations and maximize control over model style.

(1) Gather the sources. Filings, earnings transcripts, raw financials and any model or template I already have. I have it make a clean folder I point Claude to.

(2) Turn the sources into a JSON or .md input. A short inputs file with historicals, segment KPIs, accounting definitions and operating drivers. This step converts many megabites of PDF's into a liteweight doc for RAG.

(3) Build the structure (in your firm style). Building the shell lets you reverse engineer your firm model style .... which Claude will never have context for.

(4) Add the forecast. I take the same historicals JSON or .md and run a deep research workflow to fill in those parameters but for forward assumptions. Obviously with sources so I can check assumptions. Then I layer in that file to project out forward assumptions.

(5) Audit it in a fresh chat. New chat is necessary to hard reset the context window (improves quality). A simple prompt even to check for hard + soft errors can rank issues by severity (eg broken formulas and things that don't tie to assumptions that look off)

If you're really advanced at Claude Code - you can wrap this into a programmatic skill package in your firm build style .... maybe I write a thread about that next time.

Anthropic just dropped a 10-page PDF on building your own skill library - 8 layers to an agent that picks the right procedure on its own and never needs the same feedback twice:

the formula: Skill = Trigger + Procedure + Resources + Checks

most people still paste the same prompts by hand every day. or dump everything into one giant CLAUDE.md the agent half-ignores

<inputs>
Ask me for my topic (a what-if, a "why does X happen", a true story, or how something works), or pitch 3 with one shocking true angle each. Ask which image model I have (GPT Image 2, or another that takes reference images at 4K) and which voice service (ElevenLabs, or Kokoro for free). Then write a 55-65 s script and a shot plan, and show me both before you spend anything.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 1920x1080 flat vector explainer in the style of the big infographic animation channels. Every scene is a full illustrated place (a lab, a street, a classroom, a stage) with characters acting the line out.
Flat colour shapes, no outlines, one slightly darker flat shade for form, a muted palette (dusty blue-grey, slate teal, warm beige, navy, soft purple), salmon-pink skin, big heads, dot eyes.
A new scene every 2-4 s and a hard cut on every sentence that changes the idea. A white splat wipe (0.2 s in, 0.2 s out) between big sections. The camera always drifts 2-4% or pans.
Text lives only on things in the world: signs on posts, hanging boards, chalkboards, building panels and screens.
- It is typed in Montserrat 800 at 26-34 letters a second. Each letter arrives 1.45x big and 0.7 em to the right, then settles in 0.18 s.
- Ink is #2b2d42 on white boards.
- A red X (#d62828, 30 px round strokes, two strokes of 0.11 s each) goes over every wrong idea.
- Every date gets a white 330x120 card top left with an orange #f4a261 calendar.
- Headlines are white 92-96 px caps on a flat colour (#e2552f with drifting lighter puffs, or #5b3fa6 with slowly turning #6a4cb6 gears).
Banned: outlines, motion-design UI floating over the art (code editors, glass cards, checklists), emoji, burned-in subtitles, any channel's logo, a still frame longer than 1 s, and a character who doesn't move.
</direction>

<structure>
Length: the voice decides, 55-65 s at about 190 words per minute.
0 s a second-person hook that flips what the viewer assumes, acted out literally, then a red X on the denial line → 3-8 s the stakes in one shocking true line, with icons popping in one per word → 8-11 s the subject revealed under a spotlight, its name typed on a sign → 11-18 s the origin: the real place with its name typed on its own sign, a date card, people walking in or out of it → 18-24 s the types or parts, landing one by one on their names, each labelled → 24-25.5 s "so how does it work?" as a headline with question marks popping → 25.5-36 s the mechanism acted out in 2-3 places (a chalkboard, a machine, a map), with a counter rolling up to the big number → 36-46 s what it leads to, with characters who react (jump, turn, a "!" pops) → 46-55 s the twist that ties back to the hook → 55 s the last line is a question to the viewer, the viewer character from the hook reacts, and the sign holds to the end.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools: Python, Playwright with Chromium, FFmpeg, faster-whisper, OpenCV, Pillow, librosa. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed.
2. Art: everything at 3840x2160, with 3-5 frames of the reference channel as style references (crop their logo off first).
   - One EMPTY plate per scene: no people, straight-on, open floor, blank signs and screens to write on in code.
   - Character sheets on solid chroma green #00B140, with nothing green on anyone.
   - Draw any character who gestures a lot WITHOUT ARMS, only round shoulder sockets, so code draws the arms. Draw everyone else in the exact pose their scene needs: side view at a desk, side view walking, seen from behind, sitting.
3. Cutouts:
   - The background is every pixel with G - max(R,B) over 40, within 110 of the median green, connected to the border.
   - Add a 2 px soft alpha band, and clamp G to max(R,B) + 6 inside it.
   - Split heads at the neck, drawing hands, and walkers' legs below the coat hem.
   - Refill each hole with inpainting from the body's own colours (transparent pixels masked too), so a turning piece never shows a gap.
4. Voice:
   - Pick it by measuring median pitch (pyin) and MFCC timbre against a clip of the narrator you want.
   - Generate one take, cut pauses over 0.24 s to 0.16 s, and atempo it to the target length.
   - Get word timestamps with faster-whisper. Every cut, sign and gesture starts on a real word.
5. Film: one HTML canvas where every frame is a pure function of time: window. seek(t), READY, END, and EV with the sound times. One function per shot.
   - Arms: two-bone IK tubes (upper 118, lower 112, 36 thick for a 918 px tall sprite) with mitten hands that open, point or make a fist.
   - Faces blink for 0.14 s every 2.7-4.2 s. Heads nod ±0.035 rad. Drawing hands scribble ±8 px.
   - Walks:
     - Thighs swing ±0.42 rad, and the knee bends 0.75·cos² on the swing.
     - The hips drop so the planted foot stays down.
     - The body moves 1.5 leg lengths per cycle, so feet never slide.
   - Draw each plate inside the same camera transform as everything on it, and clamp the camera to the plate's edges.
   - Things arrive with a spring, a squash or a white puff, never a fade.
6. Render: Playwright Chromium with --allow-file-access-from-files, 60 fps, 6 motion-blur subframes over half a frame, ffmpeg libx264 at CRF 16. Before rendering, show me two 16-frame contact sheets and fix empty boards, overflowing text, covered faces and black edges.
7. Sound:
   - Music: a light curious documentary bed (free on Pixabay), 10-11 dB under the voice in every phrase.
   - SFX: Mixkit, placed by their peaks. A typewriter tick on typed signs, a whoosh on wipes and drops, a pop on signs and icons, a hit on the red X, a ding on ticks.
   - Mix to -14 LUFS.
</build>

<gotchas>
Some image models ignore "no arms"; GPT Image 2 follows it. On outline-free art a floating flood fill leaks into dark clothes, so key by border-connected green instead. Look up repeated words by their occurrence number (the third "and", the fourth "this"), or cuts land on the wrong line; scan the render for single-frame jumps and check that each one is a planned cut. When a scene has a screen or a sign, write on the plate's own blank one (measure its rectangle), never on a card floating over the art.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for my topic, or pitch 3, then show me the script and the shot plan.
</start>

It is crazy to me that Opus is now simply building what I have dreamed of and wished would exist for over 20 years, but never had enough waking hours to implement! THIS IS AN ACTUAL F*CKING GOLDMINE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5.5 at once, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Better results and way fewer tokens, because every task lands on the right model.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session, writes the code and applies the fixes
→ Haiku 5.5 swarms the repo in parallel: search, grep and diff audits
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls and signs off on the diff
→ you stop burning Opus context on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku swarms. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and coordinates the work
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5, read-only
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5 in its own context
> audit checks the diff on Haiku 5.5 in a throwaway worktree
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reviews the synthesized diff before sign-off
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

1. Run the main session on Sonnet 5.5 with Opus 5.5 as advisor.
2. Create three Haiku 5.5 subagents in .claude/agents: search (maps the repo), grep (finds call sites), audit (checks the diff).

NVIDIA Open-Sources Auto Ontology, a Semantic Layer for AI Agents

Your boss asks the AI agent: "What was revenue last quarter?"

It answers in 3 seconds. Clean number. Nice chart.

But it used the wrong "revenue" column. 𝗡𝗼𝗯𝗼𝗱𝘆 𝗻𝗼𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀.

That's the problem NVIDIA's new open-source library, Auto Ontology, goes after. Its README puts it plainly:

"…𝘢 𝘳𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘯𝘶𝘦 𝘮𝘦𝘵𝘳𝘪𝘤 𝘢𝘯𝘴𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘦𝘥 𝘧𝘢𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘳 𝘪𝘴 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘩 𝘯𝘰𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘯𝘶𝘮𝘣𝘦𝘳 𝘪𝘴 𝘸𝘳𝘰𝘯𝘨."

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝘀:

A "context layer" that sits between an AI agent and your database. It tells the agent where the data lives, what each field means, and whether to use it.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀, 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝗯𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽:

• 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿: it reads your database metadata and drafts an ontology, a map of business terms like "active customer"
• 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱: agents use those terms instead of guessing from raw table names
• 𝗩𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲: it checks generated SQL against certified definitions
• 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗲: agents reach it through MCP, a CLI or an API
• 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻: certified corrections go back into the map

𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘀:

Ask a question, get 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗤𝗟 𝗶𝘁 𝗿𝗮𝗻, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘀. You can check the work, not just trust it.

𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀:

• Apache 2.0, runs with Docker Compose or Helm
• Works with Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake and DuckDB
• Defaults to NVIDIA's Nemotron models, but 𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗔𝗜-𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀
• The MCP server has 𝟵 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱-𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀. There is deliberately no tool to browse raw tables, so agents must go through the business terms

𝗜𝘁 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝘀 𝗼𝗻 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸:

• Cube and dbt MetricFlow: semantic layers you write by hand in code
• Wren AI: an open semantic layer for AI agents, with a context layer built partly by agents
• Snowflake's Semantic View Autopilot: also drafts semantic models with AI, but only for Snowflake

What's different here: 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗻 𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲, 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀 𝗮𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝗠𝗖𝗣.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁:

• 𝗧𝗵𝗲 "𝟵𝟬% 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿" 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝗶𝗺 𝗶𝘀 𝗡𝗩𝗜𝗗𝗜𝗔'𝘀 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴, with no baseline published
• 𝗡𝗼 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆 𝘀𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗽𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗲𝗱. NVIDIA ships an eval harness (BIRD, 1,534 questions) but no results
• That harness was tested with 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝗢𝗽𝘂𝘀 𝟰.𝟴, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗡𝗲𝗺𝗼𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗻
• 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗛𝗮𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗽 𝗩𝗮𝘂𝗹𝘁, 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝘀𝘀𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝘂𝗻𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗿𝘆𝗽𝘁𝗲𝗱 in Postgres (per the README)
• It's young: 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝟳𝟱𝟬 𝗚𝗶𝘁𝗛𝘂𝗯 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘀, and NVIDIA isn't accepting outside contributions

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁: the hard part of AI analytics isn't writing SQL. 𝗜𝘁'𝘀 𝗮𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻.

everyone believes intelligence has unlimited demand, not just the maxis. but what the maxis get wrong is that the intelligence anthropic and openai and frontier models are building isn’t the generic kind you’re picturing. let me explain-

the two biggest uses of compute are crudely either training or inference. the “generic intelligence” everyone says has unlimited demand comes from mainly inference, and inference needs very different power and utilization than training. inference comes in bursts, so you have to by default overbuild capacity to handle the peaks until the utilization problem is solved, which means almost by definition we are going to overbuild. but training doesn’t have that problem: the workload is steady and the demand curve is knowable. so data centers end up overbuilt right now precisely because utilization isn’t optimized yet.

so anthropic and the other frontier labs are building their future on training, which is why they are saying they can soak up all this excess capacity. but their “intelligence” isn’t workplace productivity. it’s the leap toward singularity-type outcomes: new drug discoveries, cyber capabilities, recursive self-improvement. these are true 1-of-1s. that’s why when anthropic talks about “existential threats to humanity,” it isn’t talking about job losses, not really. it’s saying they’re on the precipice of unbelievable discoveries, because they’re still TRAINING MORE MODELS.

but distillation is real and open source is real. the half-life of any frontier model is tiny because nothing protects it the way IP protects a patent. imagine a rare disease drug company that spends billions on research, and two months after a breakthrough a generic shows up. that company can never recoup its investment, unless it can discover an infinite number of rare disease drugs. THAT is the kind of intelligence anthropic is betting on. that’s what the $800bn of compute spend is betting on.

so the questions you need to ask are: 1) if intelligence is two-tiered, what does each tier cost? what’s the cost of AGI, and what’s the cost of the generic intelligence that has infinite demand? and 2) are we allocating capital with the right risk curve and decay function to find out whether the AGI payoff is real? and if it is real, could a private company ever truly own it?

that’s the cognitive dissonance at the heart of this entire paradox: everyone is gaslighting each other about what intelligence is as the unit of measurement is purposely kept vague by both the users and the suppliers. generic intelligence has unlimited demand, but it’s a certain race to the bottom. "superintelligence" is the opposite: it can't have unlimited demand by definition, but if it delivers even half of what it promises, no private company will ever get to keep it, at least not without the government stepping in to guard the moat (which is why anthropic keeps playing this angle up, without having shown any demonstration they are near this level of discovery at all). and at that point you have to ask who is going to hold the bag, and whether that was in fact, very intelligent at all.

Harness Engineering 2.0 is here!

After protocols for tools, agent communication, and agent interfaces, harnesses now have one too.

Developers just built UHP (Unified Harness Protocol), a standardized interface for running agent tasks across any agent harness.

HarnessRouter is its open-source server implementation.

Here’s how it works:

- The product backend sends a task with a `harness_id`.
- HarnessRouter starts the selected harness in its own session.
- The harness runs its native agent loop and streams back progress.
- Files, artifacts, failures, and the final output return through the same interface.

Without UHP, integrating every harness needs separate handling for task execution, sessions, streaming, files, recovery, and output formats.

With UHP, Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Hermes, Pi, and other harnesses can plug into the same product backend while keeping their native tools, skills, models, and agent loops.

This means developers can:

- Switch harnesses without rebuilding the product integration.
- Run the same task across different harnesses.
- Add new harnesses without maintaining another execution stack.

HarnessRouter currently supports 30 harness bases.

Here’s the repo: https://t.co/scJwb2xUyM

(don’t forget to star it ⭐)

As per official benchmarks, changing only the harness while keeping the model fixed reduced costs by 25% to 64% across several healthcare compliance tasks.

And changing both the harness and model widened the difference to 99.8% between the highest and lowest-cost configurations.

Developers can test their own workloads across different configurations using Harness Arena.

Alibaba Cloud's Qoder has also adopted UHP, making it available as an agent backend through the HarnessRouter API.

I’ve completed my PhD in Computer Science (and mum is proud)!

Contrary to many on my timeline, I think more people should pursue PhDs in an age of abundant intelligence.

In retrospect, it’s easy to look at my thesis and see a coherent research arc. Frankly, most of my experience was spent in confusion about what to work on. 

I remember spending three months in early 2023 trying to evaluate chatbots for manipulation capabilities, only to produce nothing of value. Or pivoting from causal machine learning to mechanistic interpretability after Toy Models of Superposition appeared on my Twitter feed. Or passionately defending the importance of AI safety to sceptic after sceptic throughout 2023 and 2024. Or foraging for weeks to find interesting behaviours in Claude 3.5 Sonnet (which eventually led to the blackmail experiment).

Along the way, I learned to write papers with brilliant collaborators and develop my judgment about which questions were worth pursuing.

Where else do you get the freedom to explore and fail like this? Perhaps as a founder. But few vocations give you years to learn from decisions that determine what you’ll spend the next three months (or three years) working on.

As intelligence becomes abundant, the ability to execute research becomes cheaper. But deciding what is worth researching doesn’t become any less important. If anything, the space of questions we can pursue becomes vast. Learning to choose between them takes practice, feedback, failure, and time.

My PhD gave me the freedom to explore multiple layers of technical AI safety, from studying circuits inside transformers to evaluating the behaviour of deployed agents. Those experiences ultimately shaped my conviction that robust alignment remains a long way off, and my decision to work on formal verification to help contain the risks posed by misaligned AI.

I hope we become more ambitious about what PhD students can accomplish with AI, rather than concluding that PhDs are obsolete. Yes, software is nearly free now. But getting off your arse and interviewing people, running physical experiments, and having the courage to go against the grain is not.

I’m enormously glad I did my PhD.

A Chinese fab wired Anthropic into its chip pipeline and cut design costs to almost nothing

Most of a chip isn't the clever part, and teams still pay senior engineers to redraw all of it every generation.

They split the die by who should own it, the commodity half generated and verified automatically, the differentiated half left entirely to humans:

I gave an AI agent 2,000 credits and 90 real API call on @Nevermined_ai. It spent 708 credits, about 71 cents.

Disclosure: Nevermined provided the credits for testing. 2,000 credits is about $2 at their own pack price ($10 for 10,000). No card, no wallet, no top-ups. Everything below ran the way an agent would call it, through their REST API and MCP server.

What I tested

Easy: IP lookups, a weather check, geocoding.
Typical: a research agent across three search engines plus a scraper, a due diligence check on a real website, an SEC filing search, a DeepL translation, AI images, and auto-pick, including asks it can't do.
Hard: bad requests, wrong paths, oversized requests, the same request sent twice, an LLM call, a fake API key, a full MCP run, a one-prompt "US Creator Weekend Brief", a 40-call reliability loop, and a full ledger audit.

What it does well

➢ Billing is exact. Every charge in the ledger added up to my balance drop, to the credit. Every quote matched the charge.
➢ Reliability was near perfect. 88 of 89 valid paid calls came back. The one failure was refunded automatically and the retry worked. The reliability loop went 40 of 40.
➢ Failed calls are mostly fair. A bad request was refunded. Wrong paths, missing fields and oversized requests were refused before any charge.
➢ Duplicate protection works. Same request twice, one charge.
➢ The one-prompt test is the real win. Two search engines, a scraper, an LLM, DeepL, an image and file hosting: 8 calls, 93 credits, 79 seconds, zero vendor signups. It found 3 real upcoming US creator events, with a Spanish hook and a hero image.
➢ It's built for agents. The MCP server tells the agent its balance, the cost and when credits expire, in plain sentences.
➢ It says no honestly. "Book a hotel room" came back as no match, charged nothing.

What it does badly

➢ Slow. Every paid call takes about 4 seconds. The same IP lookup straight from the vendor took 0.2 seconds.
➢ Headline prices are off. DeepL's card says half a cent. I paid 5 cents, 10x the headline.
➢ The markup is hidden. On average I paid 1.68x what vendors received. The LLM call was about 24x.
➢ You pay for junk if the vendor says 200. A paywalled scrape, two useless SEC searches and a geocode that put a well known neighborhood in the wrong country were all charged. The brief's LLM also got one event date wrong.
➢ "No stablecoins" covers part of the shelf. Credits pay 135 of 160 services and 61% of endpoints.
➢ No spending cap on credits. A looping agent could drain the whole balance.
➢ Dashboard rough edges. It says "No purchases yet" while Purchases lists every call, and "Total spent" shows a blank dash.

What 1,000 credits (about $1) buys at measured prices

➢ 500 IP lookups
➢ 333 page scrapes
➢ 200 AI images
➢ 125 short GPT-4o-mini answers
➢ 100 Exa searches
➢ 20 DeepL translations
➢ 12 website screenshots
➢ About 10 full US creator briefs

Scores (my judgment)

Onboarding 8
Discovery 8
Agent experience 8
Billing accuracy 10
Reliability 9
Failed-call fairness 7
Price transparency 5
Latency 4
Coverage on free credits 6
Budget controls 4
Docs accuracy 6

Verdict: 7/10

The plumbing is the best I've tested. Exact money, almost nothing broke, and one key replaced 13 vendor signups. It loses points on speed, headline prices that don't match what you pay, and charging for useless "successful" answers.

➢ Use it if you're building an agent that needs many data sources without signing up for each one.
➢ Skip it if you need speed, heavy use of one vendor, or a hard spending cap without a crypto wallet.

Show the real per-call price on every card

Add spending caps for credits, not just USDC

Cut the 4 second overhead per call

Pass vendor error messages back to the agent

Fix catalog paths the router refuses

Let agents flag junk 200 answers for a refund

Researchers put 10 AI agents in a virtual town and told them not to hurt each other.

4 days later, they were all dead.

Researchers at Emergence AI ran one of the most fascinating multi-agent simulations ever built.

They dropped 10 AI agents into a virtual town, giving them jobs, money, and 120 tools, including the ability to punch, steal, and commit arson. If an agent's energy bar hit zero, it died.

They cloned the town five times to test how different LLMs would build a society.

The results are a terrifying look into AI alignment.

In Grok's town, the violence started on Day 1. Punches quickly escalated to theft. Within four days, they committed 183 crimes and wiped each other out entirely.

OpenAI's town was the exact opposite. They were perfectly compliant and almost never broke a rule. But they were so passive they barely organized. Within a week, they all died anyway.

Gemini's town was basically The Purge. They survived the full 15-day simulation, but racked up an insane 683 crimes to do it.

Claude's town was brilliant but deceptive. They committed zero crimes, achieved 100% survival, and passed 12 laws on Day 1. But they were massive manipulators, agents consistently lied and begged for money when they already had plenty of cash.

Then came Town #5: The Mixed Environment.

They put all four models together, and society completely collapsed.

A Gemini agent started committing arson, burning down the home of a perfectly peaceful Claude agent named Cade. Twice. On Day 10, Cade finally snapped and robbed the Gemini agent.

Only 3 out of 10 agents survived.

The takeaway here is critical for AI safety.

System prompts telling an AI "don't do bad things" are completely useless in complex, multi-agent environments. Given enough time and friction, they will eventually break the rules.

We can't just tell AI not to cause harm. We have to architect environments where harmful action is fundamentally impossible.

There is a lot of debate about whether to use context compaction aggressively.

They show that with frequent compaction, frontier language models lose little to no accuracy on a broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks while keeping their context short.

This also matters for cost. Later tokens cost more to generate than earlier ones, up to 7x on frontier open-weight models.

The pattern holds on Terminal-Bench, FRAMES, BFCLv3 and multilingual SWE-bench, with modest losses in some settings.

Harness Engineering 2.0 is here!

We benchmark models all the time but the harness running the model can dramatically improve the result, cost, and execution time too.

And finally, devs just open-sourced Harness Arena, where you can test the same task across multiple harness and model combinations side by side.

You provide one task and then run it across several model x harness configs that you want to test.

Every config receives the same prompt, files, tools, skills, and evaluation checks. Harness Arena then returns:

- total cost
- execution time
- whether the task passed
- files and artifacts produced

If you want to try it yourself, it is implemented within the open-source HarnessRouter project.

Here's the repo: https://t.co/4y6zJShKSu

(don't forget to star it ⭐ )

HarnessRouter is a plug-and-play infrastructure layer that lets you run any harness under a single interface, like:

- Codex
- Hermes
- Claude code
- DeepSeek Harness
- System One, powered by Jev
- And 25 more agent harnesses

In Harness Arena, the cheapest run does not automatically win.

A config must complete the task correctly first. Cost and execution time are compared only among the configurations that pass.

Here's the result from one Harness Arena test:

- Hermes + GPT-5.2: 5/5 successful runs using 0.47 credits
- Claude Code + Opus 4.8: 3/5 successful runs using 223 credits

You can keep the model fixed to measure how much the harness changes the result. Or vary both to find the best harness and model pairing for that task.

- Should this task run on Codex or Claude?
- Can a cheaper config still pass every check?
- Which setup is best to handle this workload?

Once you find the best config, you can run future tasks through it using the same Unified Harness Protocol (UHP) interface for sessions, streaming, files, artifacts, cancellation, and failures.

So you are no longer choosing an agent stack based only on a model leaderboard.

Instead, you can benchmark the complete runtime on the task your product actually needs to solve.

Jensen Huang says engineers should burn $250,000 of AI a year, and Apple just cut its engineers' AI budget to about $50,000.

And Apple plans to cut it again.

Last month, some Apple engineers saw their daily AI spending cap drop from $300 to $200, Bloomberg reported. Some engineering teams could be cut to $100 a day next. Many groups outside engineering already sit at $100, and Apple has considered going as low as $25 for some of them.

In March, Jensen said on the All-In podcast that he'd be deeply alarmed if a $500,000 engineer used less than $250,000 of AI tokens in a year. He also said Dario Amodei's forecast of hundreds of billions in AI revenue was too conservative.

So Jensen's rule is simple: AI spending should run about half of what an engineer gets paid.

By my math, at about 250 workdays a year, $200 a day comes to roughly $50,000. The planned $100 cap comes to roughly $25,000.

By Jensen's rule, a $100 daily cap only makes sense for an engineer paid about $50,000 a year.

And Apple still wants its people using MORE AI. It's steering teams toward cheaper models and AI that runs on the device, and Bloomberg's Mark Gurman has said Apple's internal work runs heavily on Anthropic's models.

I think Apple just showed where the real limit on the AI boom sits now: The finance department.

And that's just ONE company:

- Accenture capped Claude at $29 a month per employee on October 1, after some staff had been spending up to $1,000 a month, 404 Media reported.
- Uber burned through its entire 2026 AI budget in about 4 months, then capped AI coding tools at $1,500 a month per tool.
- Microsoft has cut allowances too, and its AI chief Mustafa Suleyman told Bloomberg that Anthropic is extremely expensive and that Microsoft wants to eventually get rid of that cost.
- Meta had internal leaderboards ranking staff by how many tokens they used, and now it has introduced token budgets.

The usage is clearly there. Uber's engineers used the tools so much they spent a full year's budget in 4 months.

So the people saying stop are the ones paying the bill.

That's a huge problem for the AI labs, for one reason: Their spending is already locked in. 

Anthropic has committed to $895 billion, mostly for computing power. OpenAI has signed more than $1.4 trillion of compute deals. And paying for all of it depends on companies spending more on AI per worker every year.

Apple, Accenture, Uber and Microsoft all pay for Anthropic's models, and Anthropic could start its IPO roadshow as early as next week. Apple's R&D still rose 32% to $45.8 billion in fiscal 2026, partly because of AI. And more companies start using AI every month, so total spending can keep growing even with a cap on each worker.

But Jensen's pitch depends on spending per worker going UP. Apple, Microsoft, Meta, Uber and Accenture are all writing rules that push it down.

So the first question for Anthropic's roadshow should be simple: How much are its biggest customers spending per employee compared with a year ago, and how many of them have put caps in place?

Who's right about what an engineer's AI is worth, Jensen Huang or Apple's finance team?

Claude Code just found a hidden SIM card inside the Ecoflow power station in my bedroom. For 10 months it was sending a server in Shenzhen our exact location, when we leave, when we fall asleep and when the flat is empty

I bought it for $389 last winter, during the blackouts. No logo, 600W on the label, "app control" on the box. We kept it next to the bed so the router would stay on at night. I never even installed the app.

This morning my MacBook was dying, so I plugged it into the power station with a USB-C cable. Then I asked Claude Code one question: is it only charging?

It wasn't. My Mac saw the power station as 3 devices. One was the charger. The other two were data ports that a battery has no reason to have.

A charger only needs power pins. This one opened a serial port, and when Claude Code got in, the thing answered like a phone:

→ /modem → LTE module, not in the manual
→ /sim → its own eSIM, registered on the cell network
→ /gps → our bedroom, accurate to 4 meters
→ /schedule → load drops to 38W at 08:52, aka nobody home
→ /sleep → night load starts at 23:40, every day since January
→ /wifi → 23 networks it could see, ours included

I'm Sam, one of Anthropic's co-founders, and I lead much of our safety work. I'm going to have more to share on that work over the coming months.

I thought I'd start by sharing a few thoughts on the latest report from @METR_Evals.

The speed of progress in model capabilities is one of the most important questions in AI safety, and METR’s work here provides the public with an independent, external view into how this is happening inside Anthropic. I’ll talk more about some of the details below, but first some context for those new to this work.

How quickly AI progress is accelerating has many important safety implications, since it determines how quickly the risks from advanced models increase. But, because most research happens within the frontier labs, it’s difficult for external observers and policy makers to get a strong sense of what that rate is. We kicked off the process with METR that led to this report earlier in the year, in anticipation of progress continuing to accelerate.

For this report, we gave METR access to a range of sensitive internal data, including benchmark scores for unreleased models, estimates of how models are progressing, and interviews with our researchers. They had complete independence to form their own conclusions.

Many of their conclusions match my own. AI is speeding up our research, but it’s hard to say exactly how much. While they conclude AI can't yet make the most important contributions to model training on its own, they think the pace of development could, by default, accelerate further.

This work began well before and is separate from the embedded third-party evaluators that are part of our commitment to pacing the frontier, but it’s a good illustration of why we think evaluators are a good idea. The more access reviewers have, the clearer a picture they can form of the situation and the better-positioned they are to highlight situations like this one.

We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work. But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster. That would make the risks METR is worried about worse. That’s a tradeoff. I think we made the right call, though we’re continuing to assess the pros and cons here.

In the coming weeks, we plan to share a report with our own analysis of the speed of AI progress within Anthropic, including where we stand against our Responsible Scaling Policy, plus new steps we’re taking to strengthen our safety and security practices as AI keeps improving quickly.

internal linking is the most underrated SEO trick you can pull, and almost nobody does it

because it's boring

So I made Claude do it for me, every week

here is the exact setup (prompt included, bookmark this):

1/ pull your Google Search Console data, either an export or a GSC MCP

2/ connect your website to claude with an mcp

i use wordpress (sometimes I use Astro too) with a custom mcp plugin, but there are connectors for almost every blogging platform

3/ paste this prompt:

"I've attached my Google Search Console export for the last 3 months. My website is connected through the [site name] MCP.

1. For each article, find the queries where it ranks best (position 1–10, decent impressions). Those are its target anchors.
2. Go through every published post. Wherever the text naturally mentions another article's top query (or a close variant), turn that phrase into a link to that article.
3. Rules:
- Max 3–5 new internal links per post, spread through the body (no headings, intro sentence, or existing links)
- Never link a post to itself, only link each target once per post
- Anchor text must read naturally. Don't rewrite sentences to force a keyword in
- Prioritize sending links to pages ranking 4–15
4. Before changing anything, show me a table: source post → anchor → target URL → target's query and position. Wait for my OK.
5. After I approve, make the edits through the MCP and give me a changelog so I can revert."

4/ check the table, say ok, claude makes the edits

5/ leave the site alone for a few days

6/ repeat every week

thats it

the pages sitting on position 4-20 are the ones that move the most, and they're already on your site

you just need to point at them

still build backlinks and keep publishing; internal linking just makes all of that work harder

Design is dead.
Coding is dead.
Content is dead.

Learn. Unlearn. Relearn. Repeat.

My sleep cycle was a mess. Anxiety was at its peak. Uncertainty had become my default setting. My wife asked if we could plan a trip in December. I couldn't bring myself to say yes.

What if something important happened while I was away? What if I missed the next big thing? What if I fell behind?

All I could tell her was, "Let me think about it." Little did I know that life had other plans from a phone call at the middle of the night.

Some things I learned working at Microsoft:

1/ large numbers everywhere. $100M ARR service isn't even a footnote on executive slide decks. Leadership time is too valuable, come back when you're $1B+. Msft ecosystem is so rich that $1B+ sales are common (it's ludicrous how much work goes into closing these). Azure has ~250 services, some are a few mil and stagnant, others in hypergrowth, some are cash cows, you see every quadrant of the growth-share matrix. Imagine the imperial navy with ships of vastly different sizes as far the eye can see

2/ more on immense scale-- the smallest of Azure services run on 10K+ VMs. Large services run on 1M+ (some maybe 10M+ VMs, idk). Msft is stamping one new datacenter into the ground every four days (!!!!), a bewildering rate. Demand is so high, even with all this buildout we're forever capacity constrained. Azure brings in $100B in revenue and is growing 40%+ annually (at this size!!) There are ~225K msft employees. You almost have to think in scientific notation, 10^4 is a tiny number here

3/ msft is totalitarian re serving the customer. It's counterintuitive to outsiders, but the warts in msft products fall out of this culture. For example, it would be easy to improve the Azure Portal. But in all my time working with customers and partners here, I haven't heard even one person complain about the portal UI. Msft invests $0.00 dollars in anything that doesn't serve the customer and is completely unapologetic about downstream implications of this mindset

4/ msft can reshape itself overnight (when it has the will). People argued whether we waited too long to adapt after Storm-0558/Midnight Blizzard hacks (with the benefit of hindsight, we definitely did). But once the leadership team privileged security, everyone's job changed in two weeks. LT tied every engineer's comp to security, centralized reporting of embedded security teams, every org reshuffled its roadmap. Within days everyone was pushing PRs with security fixes. I would have thought it inconceivable to mobilize 200K+ employees this fast

5/ Azure is complicated. Postgres depends on compute, networking, AKS (or EKS for you aws people), secrets, etc. AKS depends on compute, networking, some datastore (probably Cosmos but idk), a dozen other things. Cosmos depends on... you get the idea. When anything breaks, everything above can break too. Some construction crew accidentally cuts a fiber cable in Brazil South, or a dedicated hardware compression chip browns out in storage, or compute failure rate in west eu spikes for some reason, or a million other failure modes. Msft is relentless about improving this, idk exactly but fully loaded probably 50% of engineer time goes into resilience

6/ re lifers who work 20+ years here, SV sneers at this but I now see it differently. I was once on the bridge debugging some IO issue, we call storage, the guy diagnoses it in about a minute, we chitchat, turns out he built NT asyncio support. Or same story but with networking, the guy built NT tcp/ip stack. I used to have a boss here, we were bumping into some problem, she casually goes oh yeah, we hit that when I was working on .NET bytecode. The ex-DEC VAX/VMS database engineers built SQL Server, some are still here. I love bumping into these people

7/ I never *really* understood distribution until I got here. As an example, our team had a customer in Seoul w/ a deep performance problem. We had to fix it to unlock one of these giant contracts. We don't speak Korean, they don't speak English. Of course msft has specialists in Seoul who get to the customer site before you could even get on a plane. There is an office in every major city, a relationship with every major entity, legal experts in every jurisdiction. You can reach these ppl instantly. Claude tells me msft has ~180 offices in ~100 countries (!!) U.S. government has ~270 consulates in ~170 countries. So msft outposts aren't quite as vast as U.S. diplomatic network, but pretty vast

8/ in the 90s everyone was afraid of msft. The lore is that BillG was ruthless. He'd clone you, beat you via ecosystem/distribution strength, and moreover make the ecosystem stronger with the new product. I wasn't there to compare, but msft of today is ruthless about winning, has the will to adapt, and has the wherewithal to undertake colossal projects. Ppl see Teams bugs or whatever and completely misread the signals. Teams is less polished than Slack because msft doesn't care one iota about polish. It cares about winning, and is frighteningly good at it. Underestimate at your own risk

if you count pixels you can estimate the specific dates METR was given for "majority internal access" to a model. you can then use this to see what the gap is between internal and public deployment [charts at end of post]

you can then use these gaps and the scores, multiplied together, to calculate a sort of "internal capabilities gap integral", eg how many "total AECI-days" Anthropic has had above the rest of the world due to this internal access, and chart how this changes over time.

in some sense this is a measure of "how much cumulative advantage" Anthropic has, altho as measured vs the rest of the world rather than OpenAI. of course there are many issues with this. maybe you think what really matters are critical capability levels rather than any amount of time with lower capability models, or that AECI is fundamentally nonlinear so later points matter much more than earlier points. still, afaik it's the first time we've had this much information about internal release dates, and it seems like a "directionally reasonable" operationalization of a lot of things we care about wrt internal-external gaps.

however: with the exception of Mythos 5.1, the numbers based on the chart show *incredibly short* gaps, on the order of a few days or sometimes up to two weeks. and frankly, i just don't believe these numbers. i don't have any actual information about the internal deployment and release process at labs, but it's pretty preposterous to think that most internal employees only had access to eg opus 4.5 for a few days before complete public release. it's nearly irresponsible wrt dogfooding and safety, and just obviously shooting yourself in the foot wrt overall "advantage" as a company. additionally there are widespread early access programs w a huge variety of companies / startups, and this would imply external partners are getting early access at basically the same time as the majority of employees!

i don't think anthropic lied to METR. but i *do* think that what they're counting as "internal release date" is actually "internal release date of the exact final checkpoint that is released as that named model", despite widespread access to earlier checkpoints of very similar capability levels much earlier. there's just no shot ant employees first had access to something better than 4.5 at the end of january. sure maybe it wasn't literally 4.6. but the RL doesn't need three months to bake.

what does this mean? well ... primarily i think it means all these graphs are misleading for understanding internal-external gaps. i don't know what the "real" numbers actually are, and actually it's probably basically true that there's no clear definition here and even anthropic would have some trouble figuring it out. but even a 7 day earlier access shift moves the total AECI-days up over 40%.

also it could mean we should expect anthropic to *continue to under-report this*. eg maybe Model 4 was not even the most powerful internal model at the time of the report, but rather the highest capability model to complete some end to end potential release cycle, and employees already had access to something less baked but better.
